projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Patricia Wilcox was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Janice L. Friddle
sp.p: Good morning. It's September 26. We are here at Pat Wilcox's home to talk about her experience in World War II. My name is Janice Friddle. I'm here with Jeremiah Mora .. Pat, could you say good morning for us.

sp.speaker: Patricia Wilcox
sp.p: Good morning.

sp.speaker: Janice L. Friddle
sp.p: Pat what was your maiden name?

sp.speaker: Patricia Wilcox
sp.p: My maiden name was Keelan, K-E-E-L-A-N.

sp.speaker: Janice L. Friddle
sp.p: And where were you born and raised?

sp.speaker: Patricia Wilcox
sp.p: I was born in, well a suburb of Boston. And I was raised mostly in a town outside of Boston, southwest of Boston, called Dedham, D-E-D-H-A-M. It was a very old, New England town where my father and grandfather had been born and where my great grandfather settled.

sp.speaker: Janice L. Friddle
sp.p: So your family lived there for ...

sp.speaker: Patricia Wilcox
sp.p: Oh yes, generations. Yes.

sp.speaker: Janice L. Friddle
sp.p: Did you go to school after high school?

sp.speaker: Patricia Wilcox
sp.p: Oh yes. I went to Wheaton College in Massachusetts. It was then an all women's college. It had about I think 700 students. Today it's a co-ed and it has many, many more. And I went in and I graduated from high school in 1937. And that fall, I was 17, I went to college. And I majored in English literature and I graduated in '41.

sp.speaker: Janice L. Friddle
sp.p: Okay. And you currently live in Lakewood, Colorado, at 130 ...

sp.speaker: Patricia Wilcox
sp.p: At 130 South Benton Street. I've been in Colorado, I've been in Lakewood since 1954.

sp.speaker: Janice L. Friddle
sp.p: That's a long time. You're almost, you're one ofthe natives.

sp.speaker: Patricia Wilcox
sp.p: I'm a native.

sp.speaker: Janice L. Friddle
sp.p: That's right. At the time of the war, were you married, single?

sp.speaker: Patricia Wilcox
sp.p: I was single. I was semi-officially engaged to a young man from my home town that I had been going with for several years.

sp.speaker: Janice L. Friddle
sp.p: What was his name?

sp.speaker: Patricia Wilcox
sp.p: His name was John Peterson.

sp.speaker: Janice L. Friddle
sp.p: So, can you talk a little bit about how that relationship either continued or ended?

sp.speaker: Patricia Wilcox
sp.p: Well it continued when I first went into the service. And then after awhile as he was transferred out to Idaho someplace and I was transferred to the deep south, the letters became few and far between and finally they just dropped off.

sp.speaker: Janice L. Friddle
sp.p: When did you meet your spouse?

sp.speaker: Patricia Wilcox
sp.p: I met Bill Chism his name was, and I met him, he's deceased. I met him in Greenwood, Mississippi. He was a Southerner. He came from, he had been born in North Carolina and grown up in San Antonio, and I met him there. He was a cadet. He was learning to be a pilot when I met him. Janke: Okay. And, um, okay, Pat how did you become involved in World War II?

sp.speaker: Patricia Wilcox
sp.p: Well, close to you know as soon as Europe went into the War in '39, I believe - no, the last two years I was in college. From 35 to 30, from 40. I'm sorry, can you erase that part, I'm mixing up. The last two years I was in college everybody was knitting for Britain. And we knew very well that we would be soon involved in the war. Meanwhile, after I graduated I went to work for a newspaper. I had worked for this man summer times all during college and I went to work for him full time. I was a reporter. He had a string of suburban weeklies, a daily magazine, a daily paper and a couple of magazines, and I was a writer for all of those. So, anyway when they started founding the women's services, the WAC and the WAYs, that's the Woman's Navy, they were both formed approximately at the same time. And I had a brother who was a, he was in the Naval Reserve. He was at Notre Dame. He was going to be graduated as an ensign. And my father had been in the Navy. I was tempted to join the W A Vs and I loved their uniform, but they were not sending women overseas, and so I decided to go into the Army because I was very anxious to go over overseas. I wanted to see Paris which I eventually did.

sp.speaker: Janice L. Friddle
sp.p: So you got your motivations, sounded like they're kind of...

sp.speaker: Patricia Wilcox
sp.p: Well everyone, the point is that everyone was gone. I mean all the fellahs were gone. They were either drafted or they enlisted. One of my brothers just dropped out of high school his senior year. He had already gone into the service. The other one that I just mentioned was at Notre Dame, was ready to be commissioned. And all their friends were gone, and it was very, very boring. It really was. Without all our friends, we had millions of friends that were at our house all the time. And they were all going off and it was very dull. And my boyfriend had gone off in the Navy. And, anyway I was very intrigued by this idea of a great adventure really.

sp.speaker: Janice L. Friddle
sp.p: Wonderful. Wonderful. So, tell us where you first, once you joined what happened?

sp.speaker: Patricia Wilcox
sp.p: Well, my best friend - I would have joined the minute it was formed in 1942. It was formed May - it was legalized on the 151h of May 1942, and then they started recruiting. And I would have gone, but my best friend wanted to go too, but her father was very death against it. He thought it was a horrible thing for a young woman to do. And finally, it took us months to talk him into it. But finally we did talk him into it, and so she and I both were sworn in together in February '43 in Boston. And, we then went off two weeks later to basic training in Fort Oglethorp, Georgia. Janke: What was that like? What was basic training?

sp.speaker: Patricia Wilcox
sp.p: It was horrible. It was horrible. They had, you know, I mean I pictured myself all dolled up in this uniform which they weren't the greatest uniforms. But they had no uniforms. And I had gotten - everybody dressed up to get on this troop train. There were about a couple hundred girls in New England going down. And I wore a fur coat and a beautiful blue velvet suit that I had with a white blouse and my high heel shoes, and so forth, so anyway we went on this awful troop train down to Chattanooga, Tennessee and then some trucks met us. And we had to crawl into the trucks. And it took us about 15 minutes just to cross the state line and get to Fort Oglethorp, Georgia. When we got there, they took my coat and my hat and my high heels and they shipped those home, and I was left in the blue velvet outfit. And all they had to give us in uniforms was a man's, they called it a mackinaw, but it fell all the way to the ground. And then they had very long, oxford shoes that laced up and had low heels. They were terrible, I mean they made your foot looked like a gun boat, and they were horrible looking. And they, I mean they were old lady shoes, and that's what we wore. And I wore that blue velvet while I was scrubbing floors. I wore the blue velvet while I was on kitchen police, which is called KP. I wore it peeling tons of potatoes, cleaning grease traps in the mess hall kitchen. I wore it for every single duty that we had. And it was wrecked.

sp.speaker: Janice L. Friddle
sp.p: So the Army at that time was only prepared to give you shoes and basically an overcoat?

sp.speaker: Patricia Wilcox
sp.p: Yes, that's all. It was a man's overcoat. And we wore those things. And the basic training consisted of a lot of marching. Most of us didn't know our left from our right. And we had to fall out of, they called it fall out. That means get up. And we had to fall out of bed I think around 5:30 in the morning and go outside and do physical training, exercises. And then we all had to learn to march, and then we went to classes. And we studied things like how to read a map in case you're suddenly in the Sahara Desert with no one. I mean I can't imagine any such thing, but we learned. And hygiene. They showed movies that had been made for men about venereal diseases. And it was really geared towards the men's classes. You know there was really nothing in particular that was suited to women. They were still trying to feel their way through.

sp.speaker: Janice L. Friddle
sp.p: Well that must have been, in a way, very fascinating just to be kind of pioneering new ground.

sp.speaker: Patricia Wilcox
sp.p: Well it was. Yeah, we were pioneers. Yeah we were. And the assortment of girls was spectacular. I mean there were a lot of college grads, and then there were a lot of girls that had never gone to high school. But you had to pass - the first thing you did when we got off the train and into the camp, the first thing they did with us was take us into a room and we all took tests, intelligence tests, IQ tests, test to find out what our abilities were and that kind of thing. And so we worked all the time. At night we had to shine shoes. Everyday we had to stand inspection. Our ties had to be - we did have a tie that I wore over my blue velvet which was kind of ridiculous. But we had to learn to tie them you know. And we had to stand inspection by our bunks. I mean there were two, they were double decker bunks. And you couldn't look - the officer that was inspecting you, you weren't allowed to look them in the eye. You just had to look at their chest. I always felt that if! looked him in the eye I'd burst out laughing, but then they wanted to see how shiny your shoes were. And if your stockings were pulled up correctly, cotton stockings I might add. And just if your bed, if they could toss a quarter on it. It had to be very tight. And if your floor was scrubbed. And that kind of thing.

sp.speaker: Janice L. Friddle
sp.p: So you're in the same blue suit everyday for two weeks?

sp.speaker: Patricia Wilcox
sp.p: Yeah. Well the basic training was four weeks and I think I was in the blue suit for about three with the mackinov. And then they came along and they gave us what they called a physical training dress, and it was a seersucker dress with little, some had brown stripes and some had little green stripes on them. And with them we had a pair of bloomers that matched. Ha, ha, ha. That were hilarious. We had many a laugh over these things.

sp.speaker: Janice L. Friddle
sp.p: So you were the first in fashion in the Woman's Army Corp?

sp.speaker: Patricia Wilcox
sp.p: Oh absolutely. Oh yeah, we were gorgeous.

sp.speaker: Janice L. Friddle
sp.p: Yes. Okay so you finished basic.

sp.speaker: Patricia Wilcox
sp.p: Yeah, I finished basic and then in basic training we knew that all of us would be assigned to some kind of work. And I had this horrible dread, after having so much KP and some of those cooks were pretty rough. And I had this horrible dread that I'd be sent to cooks and baker school. I had never cooked a thing in my life. My mother didn't believe in teaching me how to cook because she was a lousy cook anyway, and she thought every girl should marry some man that could hire a cook. And in those days, you know, household help was very cheap. So, I lived in dread of going to cooks and bakers. Now one thing that happened was that the menus that every Army camp followed had been designed for men. And the meals were humongous. And all of a sudden all these WACs starting gaining - I was underweight when they let me in, but I was soon zooming up there. I was about 120 by that time. I think I had been 108 or something when I joined. So anyway, after basic I was sent with my friend, Francis Delaney, who was my childhood friend that had gone in with me, we were sent to a place called the casual detachment at Fort Oglethorp. There was a bunch of just wooden barracks. And we had to sit there waiting everyday to find out where we were going, and we were there for about, I think we were there ten days just sweating it out wondering what was going to become of us, and then someone came down and told us we were going to radio mechanics school. Now how I became a mechanic I have no idea because I can't fix a thing. And, but she also passed, so we went to radio mechanics school for 13 weeks up in Newark, New Jersey. And we went, just before we left, they issued us summer uniforms. Georgia was terribly hot. And they didn't fit well at all, but anyway we piled into a train and up we went. We were the first group to go to this place called the United Radio and Television Institute which is very, very impressive. And we had to learn all about electricity, which I never understood, and how to fix - and then we had to build, in order to pass this test, we had to build something called a superheterodyne radio and that would work. Well we lived in an old hotel that was very near the railroad stations and we were the first WACs to go to this hotel, the Saint Francis. It was a very non-descript hotel. It was filled with elderly people who had rooms there and they were gradually moving these people out, so it was a seven story building and we were on the seventh floor. My friend Delaney and two other gals, and we had a blast. The four of us, we had a wonderful time. And, I don't mean to get into the drinking very much, but in those days people drank a lot more than they do now. And there was an elevator boy, he was about 8 years old. And we'd give him money to go down to a liquor store and buy us booze. And then the whole floor, all of us had been in basic together, the whole floor would sit around and have parties. So those were the nights when we very often we were restricted to the hotel for the night. And then in the morning we'd march off to classes, radio school.

sp.speaker: Janice L. Friddle
sp.p: That's a great - I like that addition. Thank you, that was kind of special. So what happened when you finished school?

sp.speaker: Patricia Wilcox
sp.p: together. Well, when we finished school the Army had told us, we asked the Army if we could stay

sp.speaker: Jeremiah Mora
sp.p: Are you okay?

sp.speaker: Patricia Wilcox
sp.p: One nice thing about Newark was that the train station was right down the street. If we got an A on our weekly exams, we were able to take the weekend off, so I was always on that train going up to Boston. And, to see my family. I have a big family. And, we went into New York a great deal because it was only, you just go through the tunnel on the train and we were into New York. And the people were marvelous. We'd go in, the four of us, to a restaurant. And when we go to pay our bill, they'd say your bill was paid by a couple sitting over there. This happened all the time, all the time. We got so that we were really - we'd go into a place without any money knowing that somebody would buy us a meal, you know when we were in New York or down in Greenwich Village or wherever we happened to be. The people were just great. And in Newark, I wanted to bring up one thing about Newark, New Jersey. We paraded between - whenever there was a baseball game, we paraded. Whenever there was a parade, we paraded. And we paraded through a little park to go to school everyday. And the people would stand there and clap, and they were perfectly marvelous until toward the end ofthis 13 weeks, some chain of newspapers wrote a column stating that the intention of the WACs was to fulfill the sexual needs of the soldiers and that they were issued birth control pills which didn't even exist. And I remember the day that article came out. It was in a morning paper, and that day all the people that used to sit in that park, none of them looked at us. It was just horrible. I mean we didn't know what had happened, but usually all these people would clap as we went through. There were a lot of old men playing dominoes along the park you know. They just turned the other way.

sp.speaker: Janice L. Friddle
sp.p: So all of a sudden you went from being heroes ...

sp.speaker: Patricia Wilcox
sp.p: We went from being heroes to being, you know, prostitutes really. It was very bad. My father was a good friend of Edith Nourse Rogers, that middle name is spelled N-O-U-R-S-E, and she was the congresswoman who really backed this whole WAC bill and got it through, got it approved. And he was a friend of hers, and he went down to Washington to see her, to tell her that he would not tolerate this talk about the WACs, and of course they found that it was sometimes it was, not back home but in the various towns where the WACs were situated. The women really were upset because I mean here were all these strange women taking their men and then there was a bunch of, people were selling uniforms that looked like WAC uniforms that any civilian could buy, and so all these hookers were buying these uniforms and hanging around the gates of Army posts and none of that helped, you know.

sp.speaker: Janice L. Friddle
sp.p: No. I never even knew that.

sp.speaker: Patricia Wilcox
sp.p: Yeah, yeah. The civilians, it was a great scandal. A lot of it was soldier talk. A lot of them did not like the WACs because we were meant to replace them so they could go overseas and fight. And they were preferably content to stay right where they were. So, the slogan of the WAC was a WAC is in back of you. They didn't like that at all because they were being shoved into combat. So most of them were very nice about it. Others were very bitter.

sp.speaker: Janice L. Friddle
sp.p: It's just kind of amazing to hear the social stigma that got attached to something.

sp.speaker: Patricia Wilcox
sp.p: Oh yeah. It was bad. It was bad. But it did clear up after awhile, but the gals did a great job. So after that I went to some radio school, I was sent down to place called Greenwood, Mississippi. Worst place that I ever lived. And very, very southern. Very southern. And they didn't like northerners there, and they were still fighting the Civil War which they call the War of Northern Aggression. The older generations, say my parents generation. They weren't very kind when they heard a New England voice like mine. And, I mean I never knew, I never thought of myself as a Yankee, but that's what I was called all the time, that Yankee woman. But, anyway, I went down there, and it was a small company and it was nice. And I worked in the radio shack down there. I am not mechanical at all. Most men had to help me with everything. I didn't know what I was doing. And we had to wash all the radio parts all the time in carbon tetrachloride. And after several months I became deathly ill from all this inhalation. It's a very dangerous, you know they don't use it anymore. But we were drenched in carbon tetrachloride all the time. But we fixed the radios, we get them onto the basic trainer planes. Bring them in the shop, fix them up and put them back and test them out. That was that job. Sometimes I worked day shifts, sometimes I worked night shifts. And our uniform at that, of course by that time I had a full uniform. But what we wore were the men's overalls, coveralls.

sp.speaker: Janice L. Friddle
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Patricia Wilcox
sp.p: Getting sick on tetrachloride.

sp.speaker: Janice L. Friddle
sp.p: Okay. When you got sick after working with the tetrachloride, what happened next?

sp.speaker: Patricia Wilcox
sp.p: Well, when I first went into the service and was tested and everything, I was told that I really should be in public relations because I had been, you know, writing. And I had been writing all my life really. And I didn't want to get in at Fort Oglethorp because I knew I'd be stuck there forever. And, but I was very amenable to public relations work. So when I got sick, some major came from Maxwell Field. I belonged to something, our field was attached to something called the Eastern Flying Training Command. And it took in all the southern states from Florida over to the border of Texas and then up I think through North Carolina. It had loads and loads of airfields that were under it's direction. The head was at Maxwell Field, Alabama. So this major, woman major came to Greenwood and talked to me about my experiences as a newspaper woman. And she said I'm reclassifying you to public relations and she said you'll be shipped to Maxwell Field within the next few weeks. They need more people because of course the men, they wanted to send the men out to work on Stars and Stripes which was the Army newspaper that was put out everywhere.

sp.speaker: Janice L. Friddle
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Patricia Wilcox
sp.p: And which was the Bible. I mean that's the only newspaper we ever saw. So they needed . women. So that's what happened to me. I went to Maxwell Field. And I had a great time there. I worked with you know great guys. They were newspaper people and the minute they put me on KP down there, by that time I was a PageS three stripe sergeant. And when they - I'd say to them, I have to do KP tomorrow. You're not doing any KP, no more KP. Call back the commanding officer. I don't want her on KP. I don't want her on parades. I don't want her on any of this special duty nonsense that you people put up with. She is here to work and she's to be here everyday. And so that got me out of all this other goop that I had to go through. And they were all newspaper men. I mean they were a great bunch. So we had a lot of fun. We put out a monthly, almost a magazine that incorporated news that had been sent in from all the different fields and a lot of it had to be rewritten and edited and headlined. We laid out the paper and so forth. The officers didn't do much but the enlisted, there were four of us enlisted there.

sp.speaker: Janice L. Friddle
sp.p: How long were you at Maxwell?

sp.speaker: Patricia Wilcox
sp.p: I was there for quite awhile. As I recall, I was there for about a year which is a long time. Because they shifted people around a lot. But, you see when I was in Greenwood, I had met this cadet. I met him on a bus. We were not allowed, the enlisted women were not allowed to date officers unless they were married to them, or to date any of the cadets. I mean we were not to go near these people and they weren't to come near us. But anyway, I met this cadet on a bus and we got talking and I was bemoaning the fact that I didn't have enough coat hangers or something, and he said I've got plenty of them, so he said let me get you some. So anyway, we started dating. And the whole thing became quite serious and then he shipped out to go to another flight school down in Columbus, Mississippi, and I'd get a pass and go down and see him. And then when I landed in Maxwell Field, it was in January '44, he was also there for his final bomber training. He was a B24 pilot. So, there we were again. you know together. which was wonderful. I mean I never expected that to happen. It was just very unlikely. So we became engaged at that point and he gave me a ring. And then I had to go to the commanding officer and show her my ring, and he had to come with me and say that yes we were engaged. And we were going to get married some day. he didn't know and neither did I. And, then she had to write out a permission that Sergeant Patricia Keelan had permission to date Lieutenant William Chism. So I had to show that to the MPs every time the MPs would come up and say, do you have a pass to be with this man, with this officer? Yes and I'd take it out of my wallet and show it to them. It was ridiculous.

sp.speaker: Janice L. Friddle
sp.p: And so, how long was he at Maxwell Field?

sp.speaker: Patricia Wilcox
sp.p: Well he was at Maxwell Field I think until about June, something like that. Then he was transferred. let's see when was VB Day? He was transferred to Savannah, Georgia. And just before VB Day he called me up and he said to me let's get married. Why don't you come - see if you can get time off to come to Savannah, we'll get married. So I went to the you know the General that was in charge of my thing and I said I want a pass. I want to go to Savannah, Georgia. I want to get married, I'm getting married. And, the fellow looked at me and he said if you're going to get out of here, you better get going right now. He said I want you leaving right now. Go home, pack and get into town and get on a bus, and. or a train or whatever. I've forgotten whether I went by train. I think I went by train. And, I thought well, what is he brushing me off so quickly for? Well D-Day was coming. He knew it because our office, it was connected with intelligence. It was part of the intelligence department. And he knew that it was going to be D-Day the next day. and that all the bases would be closed down and nobody would be moving. So the only people moving were the people that were actually moving on trains or buses or cars or whatever. So anyway. of course I had no idea what was going to happen. nor did my husband. So we were married down there in a cathedral. I was a Catholic and he was not. And I had to laugh at my mother who was very Catholic indeed. We married at this cathedral called the Cathedral of St. John the Baptist, well when she sent out wedding announcements she left the Baptist out because she [LAUGHTER] Cathedral of Sant John, and forget the Baptist. But I didn't have my baptismal certificate with me, but this priest agreed to marry us and then that night he called up the priest where I had been baptized to verify that I was baptized.

sp.speaker: Janice L. Friddle
sp.p: So was the plan that your husband would convert at some point, or was that not even an issue?

sp.speaker: Patricia Wilcox
sp.p: Well, no, I had to promise to bring up the offspring in the Catholic faith. And he had to degree which was no big deal because neither one of us was particularly interested in religion anyway. By that time, I had really left the Catholic church. My mother didn't know it, but I knew it.

sp.speaker: Janice L. Friddle
sp.p: So then what happens?

sp.speaker: Patricia Wilcox
sp.p: So then I went back to Maxwell. And then he went to Hampton, Virginia, and that's before he went overseas, and I was able to get, wangle more time and go up and see him there. And, they were very good about that kind of thing. And then he took off overseas. And he wound up in Italy where he was pilot with the 15th Air Force. And he was - he did a lot of flying over Europe, bombing flights over Europe. And then they transferred him on some kind of a special mission to Algiers, North Africa. I don't know what he was doing there. I never have been able to find out. And he was on a plane that crashed. Janke: Oh, I'm sorry.

sp.speaker: Patricia Wilcox
sp.p: He was killed. So that was very sad.

sp.speaker: Janice L. Friddle
sp.p: So where were you when you learned that your husband had been in a plane crash?

sp.speaker: Patricia Wilcox
sp.p: I was at Maxwell Field. Janke: Still at Maxwell. Pa Yeah. Yeah. They called me - my commanding officer called the commanding officer of my division and told him. So he came, he sent his secretary and she said you're wanted. Lieutenant Reed wants to see you, or Captain Reed or whatever she was. So I thought, now what have I done? You know I thought I'm in trouble somehow. I've done something. I've left stockings somewhere or I messed up something. But I never expected that. But anyway, that's what it was.

sp.speaker: Janice L. Friddle
sp.p: That must have been very hard because you were married ...

sp.speaker: Patricia Wilcox
sp.p: It was very difficult because we hadn't been married all that long you know. So they gave me a leave and the Lieutenant or the Captain I think she was really, she called my father up and told him. So my father was he was a lawyer. He was the senior partner in a big law firm in Boston, and he and my mother immediately made plans to come down to Georgia to his mother's house where I also went. That's when I met his mother for the first time. Janke: After his death?

sp.speaker: Patricia Wilcox
sp.p: Yeah. And his sisters and his little brother, yeah. So, anyway my folks came down. I thought it was very nice of her. I think they were Episcopalians but she had a mass for the sake of my mother and father. She had a mass. the memorial mass in the Catholic church which I thought was very nice.

sp.speaker: Janice L. Friddle
sp.p: Very considerate.

sp.speaker: Patricia Wilcox
sp.p: Yeah. Yeah. So I just loved her. She was only - she must have married when she was 18 or something because she was only 20 years older than I, and we were very much alike. And we shared many of the same interests. She loved to read, I did too. She had majored in English, I had too. So we were just best friends right away. And I saw a lot of her up to the time I remarried and came here. And in fact she even came out here to visit. Janke: So at what point do you get to go overseas?

sp.speaker: Patricia Wilcox
sp.p: Well, after - when my father was at Maxwell Field and my mother-in-law and the family were living down in Maltry, Georgia, this young man - most of the new public relation officers had to go to Maxwell Field to report and to get sized up and found out if they were, you know whether they were any good or not. And this young man came in, he was very nice guy. And he was a Lieutenant Shannon, he came from New Orleans. But anyway, he found he was going down to Spence Field which was in Maltry, Georgia where my in-laws lived. So I said to him one day when we were talking, I said if you get down to Maltry, if you need somebody why don't you call for me. So he did. As soon as he got down there, he asked for me to be transferred. They needed a new editor for the paper. The male editor of the paper was being shipped overseas. So I went down to Spence Field and I became the editor of the paper, the weekly paper that they put out down there. Every air base had its own newspaper you know. And so that was interesting work because a lot of the combat people were coming back and I was interviewing a lot of them. And I really, you know of course I lived in the barracks naturally, but I saw my innlaws quite a bit. And we had a good time together. So I was there when, I was at Spence Field when Roosevelt died. And I had known a girl in Maxwell Field who was more or less in charge of shipping people out. And she and I were very good friends. And, I told her if ever they get a call for a public relations person to go to Europe, don't forget me. So I wasn't there too long when my orders came in that I was go to overseas. So I went to Fort Des Moines, Iowa, which was the very first training center they had for basic center the WACs had. It was an old Calvary post so they used those old Calvary posts. And I went there for, I think it was two or three weeks overseas training. And overseas training amounted to running through woods throwing grenades, which had nothing to do with anything. And more lectures about foreign countries and how you should learn to speak part of the language and so forth, and how to behave in different countries. And then one day they had this huge frame, it went up about 100 feet in the air, and it was netting, it was cargo netting line. So that was the last thing we had to do. We had to climb up to the top of the cargo netting and then down the other side. That's in case we get in a shipwreck. So I have this hideous fear of heights. And I started to go up it and this major was standing there watching me and I think I got up about maybe this high. I said I can't do this. I absolutely cannot do it, I won't do it. She said well then you can't go overseas. And I said well, so be it. I said it terrifies me and I'm not going to go up on this thing. Well, they overlooked it. But ironically I got into a shipwreck on my way home and I thought I was going to have to go up one of those things. But, to me it seems so non-sensible. Why would I have to climb a cargo net, you know? But anyway, we get out of there. I went over to - I sailed to New York on the original Queen Elizabeth I which later burned you know.

sp.speaker: Janice L. Friddle
sp.p: So you went over on the Queen Elizabeth I?

sp.speaker: Patricia Wilcox
sp.p: Yeah I went on a troop train, from Iowa to New York and went right immediately on Queen Elizabeth I. And it was a beautiful ship. It had been refitted as a troop ship, and so all the railings around this vast ship were all carved of people's initials and hometowns and all this kind of thing. The soldiers had all carved the thing up. And I was - the cabins were large. They were beautiful, but they were outfitted with bunk beds at this point. And I think I was in with about six or seven other girls. I've forgotten. But one night, I met a girl on a train, I'll never forget her. Her name was Harriet Gray and one day she came up to me and she said I have met some very interesting people, and I said who are they. She said they work in the pharmacy here on this ship. And I said, so? She said, they make booze. I said oh. We couldn't drink there, I mean. So she said let's go down and visit them tonight. So I finally said okay. So anyway, the two of us went down and we chatted with these fellows. They were nice guys and we had several of the homemade, home brew that they had cooked up. And I tell you we were both in horrible shape. Not only did we not get in bed on time, because at night they checked you every single night. Every camp I went to, at 11 o'clock somebody came through to make sure you were in bed. And of course, you had to be there in the morning. And it was way passed 11 o'clock and we had missed bed check. And Harriet Gray and lland they had these beautiful marble staircases in this ship. And Harriet and I staggered up these two flights of marble stairs, holding on to one another so nobody would - and standing at the top, who was there but one of the majors. And she said, well you're a beautiful sight, the two of you. She said you're going to hear about this in the morning. So, [LAUGHTER] we were called in and told that we were likely to get court marshaled when we got to France. But, she said, in the meantime the two of you are going to stand watch. Now standing watch meant that you had to get up at midnight, go out on the deck, it was freezing cold, and stand watch. And standing watch meant looking for something bobbing in the ocean, I don't know what we were supposed to be looking for. There were a few, you know, bombs still scattered around but not many. So anyway, I went through that every night for the rest of the time as punishment for getting drunk. But, then they forgot this court marshal thing. They never really knew about it, but we landed in Scotland and then we took two trains down through Scotland into England [UNINTELLIGIBLE]. And into England and then we got on old troop ships and went over to France.

sp.speaker: Janice L. Friddle
sp.p: So what year then, or at what time of the year did you arrive in France?

sp.speaker: Patricia Wilcox
sp.p: Let me think. It was right after the VB Day. That was May, so it must have been June. And we took the troop train and then of course we took this boat, a horrible boat, over to France and got on another train. And it kept stopping. I was so fascinated by the French landscape. All along the tracks were these children. And they all had their hands out. They wanted food. And there was one girl who annoyed me no end, she was giving them pennies. I mean they couldn't do anything with money. They needed food. They wanted gum. They wanted apples. They wanted whatever they could get. So whatever we had and we were on something called sea rations that we - I mean they didn't want to put a dining car on this thing of any kind, and so we each had a box of sea rations, cheese and crackers and that kind of thing. So we gave those to the kids because you know we didn't need them. It was all we could give them. I mean we didn't have any fresh food or anything like that. But it was pretty desolate, but I loved France. And, anyway, they took us to a place called, and I don't know how to spell it, it's Compiegne. And I think it's C-O-M-P-E-I-G-N-E if I'm not mistaken. It's where the Armemeste of World War I was signed. And there was a beautiful, beautiful chateau there. And the train tracks went right in there and that's where they had all met to end World War I. And we were there, of course we weren't in the chateau. That's where the officers were, but we were in tents there. And I've got to tell you that we ate from all this time, we ate from tin trays, everywhere we went. I mean, at the base camps we all had tin trays. We never saw china or anything like that, or any kind of dishes. And it was compartmented, you know. And so you'd get up there, well I'm thinking of coffee, and you'd get up there and they'd slop the ice cream on top of the peas and that kind of thing and meat loaf. It was, the food was good, but it all was junked together. You know the hot was next to the cold and everything melted and it all got cold. And then after you finished eating this stuff with, you had a little mess kit of your own to carry with you all the time, and after you finished you had to take the trays and dip them into these barrels of steaming hot, blue water. And I guess the blue was something that, you know, eradicated the germs. So anyway, while I was there, they had a bus going in. It was like another what they call staging area. They were sending girls into Germany. They were sending girls into different places. And when I say girls, these were women, today they call women, but we always called each other girls. And I was hoping I didn't have to go to Germany. I really wanted to go to Paris. And I went in one day and they offered a bus trip to Paris and I went in to sightsee. But I had a friend that I had known at Maxwell Field who was stationed there. So I gave her a call when I got there. I knew where she was working. And she and I did a bus tour, you know Napoleon's tomb and so forth. And, I said to her - she said, you've got to find work in the building I'm in. She said it's the old Shell Oil building, so she said see if you can find ajob there when you get here. And you can room with me. So, anyway, a few days later I got my orders to go to Paris. I went and saw her and moved in more or less, and I really had to look for a job. I went to the Shell Oil Building and I found that there was a place called information and education. And information education was at that time the war in Europe was over you see, although it was still going on in Japan. And, all these GIs that had been through combat, they had been all over the place. They didn't know what to do with them and of course a lot of them were getting into all kinds of trouble, raising hell, and getting drunk and just being obnoxious to the French people. So they set up this wonderful education program. You could, if you wanted to learn to be a chef, you could go and work with these master chefs in the French restaurants and learn from them. Or if you were interested in design, I don't know what guys - I guess there was some. I mean they worked with the famous designers. Or if they wanted to go to the Suborn and take the classical course, they could and stay as long as they wanted on the government. And of course a lot of them did this because they figured as long as I'm in this course, I'm not going to get shipped over to Japan you know. And anyway, the shipments were very slow because they just didn't have enough transport. They didn't fly people in those days. They flew the officers, but there weren't that many planes. I mean everybody went by boat, slow boat usually. And so these fellahs were very anxious to, you know these guys that were around Paris were anxious to stay there. So anyway, I worked in information education. I had to write stories about the different programs they had. Once in awhile administrative people would come over, especially women, I'd go out on a jeep with them and take them to these different schools. And I wrote speeches for the commanding officer and you know, this kind of thing. I worked with a bunch of newspaper men. [END OF SIDE A]

sp.speaker: Patricia Wilcox
sp.p: And I lived in a wonderful, small hotel, residential hotel. It was just absolutely lovely with my friend Emily who I had known at Maxwell Field. And of course it was totally different there because you actually had a maid for a change. I mean we didn't make our beds. We didn't have to do anything. I mean there was nothing like KP. We ate in the hotel next door and we had our meals there next door, I've forgotten the name, the Windsor Hotel I think it was. The one I was in was called the Rafael, and it was very close to the yard and very close to the ships basically. And life was pretty free. I never did meet the commanding officer there. And of course, there was so much to do in Paris, and some of the fellahs that I worked with and I would go out at night and just roam around, and we walked over to the Latin Corridor and almost every night I'd see Gertrude Stein and her friend Alice Tolklis and their dog. And then Marlene Dietrich used to pop into our office quite often to see the major, and she and the major would go out drinking. And of course every time Marlene Dietrich came in, she'd sit on the major's desk and all these men that I worked with would all get up and make an excuse to leave the office so they could look in and see Marlene legs you know. So we had a lot of writers and so forth coming over then to do stories on Europe as it was then beginning to bounce back. Paris, the people had plenty of money, but they didn't have anything to buy. And in the dining room where we ate, it had large plate glass windows and it was really horrible because as we ate our meals, there would be people standing there watching us eat. So all of us got involved in the black market, everyone of us. And mostly food. My father used to send me packages from Boston, you know from a very nice store in Boston, filled with cheeses and that kind of thing. I'd sell them. I mean they wanted to get, the only soap they wouldn't buy was the Lifebuoy. I don't know whether you know Lifebuoy soap, but it was kind of red and it smelled as though it was antiseptic smelling and of course the French loved perfumes and colognes and they wouldn't touch Lifebuoy even though it made them smell totally sanitized. And I sold, well we all sold stuff.

sp.speaker: Janice L. Friddle
sp.p: Was that considered taboo by the ...

sp.speaker: Patricia Wilcox
sp.p: Oh, no, of course it was taboo.

sp.speaker: Janice L. Friddle
sp.p: Okay. So when you talk about it being a black market, it was in fact against the rules.

sp.speaker: Patricia Wilcox
sp.p: It was a black market. It was against the rules. But I had an extra pair of shoes that I didn't want, and I sold them I think for $20, something like that. And people would come up to you, and we had a very large PX, huge place. It's now a mammoth Woolworth I think. But we could get cigarettes for a dollar a carton. And French people would be hanging around there, come up and say cigarettes. You know, combia, how much the cigarettes? And we'd sell it to them for maybe $5, which cigarettes, anything that we could get. Anything, they wanted to buy. And also the American Legion had it's headquarters there and they set up a hamburger stand really in part of their building. They had a beautiful home there. And the hamburgers, it was for the GIs really to go there. But this fellah and I would go down almost every day to get hamburgers -for all the other fellahs in the office. And I a had rain hat that was quite voluminous, and I'd fill that up. I think the hamburgers were a dime a piece, maybe a nickel a piece. I've forgotten, very cheap. We'd go down there and get them for the office and then I'd put a napkin down and then I'd load up on more. And this was along the street, we just handed them out to these people. They loved them. They were really having a tough time.

sp.speaker: Janice L. Friddle
sp.p: In the stories that you've told so for, I mean you certainly had some personal experiences that were tragic, and you also talked about things that you observed. One of the things that occurred to me was that in all of the contact that you had, I have to imagine that there were people who didn't fair as well as you did as far as travel.

sp.speaker: Patricia Wilcox
sp.p: Oh no. No. No.

sp.speaker: Janice L. Friddle
sp.p: Can you talk a little bit about that?

sp.speaker: Patricia Wilcox
sp.p: Well, a lot of the girls left. When we joined it was the Women's Army Auxiliary Corps. And we had joined with the understanding that we never be considered veteran's. We would never get veteran's rights. We were not really Army, we were attached to the Army. We'd have to pay our own hospital bills, we'd never get anything. But we didn't care. A lot of us didn't care. But aside from that, that we could go overseas. Now the W A Vs, they were taken right into the Navy. They were an integral part of the Navy, but they were never to go overseas. And so, a lot of the girls went to terrible camps. I mean camps down in southern Louisiana where it was nothing but bugs and swamps and everything like that. And they either deserted or they just - when the Army finally in September, I had been in about six months, they finally made us part of the Army. We all had to re-enlist. And they lost about 20 percent of the women that had enlisted. And some of them were just absolutely hated it. They hated the duties that we had to do. They hated their commanding officers or they hated the camp, or they just didn't like to be told what to do every minute. There was something, it occurred to me the other day when I was thinking about it, it seems to me that very unpleasant things that happened. You just kind of put yourself on automatic pilot and you did it. I had to go through a gas chamber one day, and evidently my gas mask wasn't on correctly. And I got a good dose of gas, and right after that I had to stand for an hour at attention on a parade ground and I almost passed out. And I could feel myself going. And I knew that if I fell on the ground, they would just keep standing, and they'd walk away. You just had - so I had two of the gals held me up. And I don't even remember leaving the parade ground you know. Now there were girls that became pregnant. And, they were just immediately sent home. Sent - they never went home. They always sent someplace else, because they didn't want their folks to know about it. I mean, unmarried gals getting pregnant. And there were just a lot of unhappy people that just dropped out, that felt why should I work for $50 a month. The pay originally had been $21 a month but when I went in it had been turned to fifty. Why should I work for $50 a month when I can be in the defense industry you know. And lot of them had parents die and they give them sympathetic discharges and so forth.

sp.speaker: Janice L. Friddle
sp.p: Of the women that became pregnant, did most of those women marry or did they - was there was sudden surge in adoptions?

sp.speaker: Patricia Wilcox
sp.p: I don't know what they did. I had a friend, well she wasn't really a close friend, but a woman I knew when I was at Maxwell Field became pregnant, she got involved with one of the soldiers there and I guess he was probably married, but whatever, it was just one of those things. And she did not want to tell her mother where she was going, but she told me. She said I'm going to be shipped out at midnight. And she said I'm going to give you my mother's address and she said, you know and where I'm going to be. She was going to Florida to live. And she said, so would you forward my mail to my mother and then I'll write letters, and will you mail them to my mother to me. So I kept that charade up until I left Maxwell Field, then I had to tell her I couldn't do it anymore. So I don't know what she told ...

sp.speaker: Janice L. Friddle
sp.p: Do you know what happened to her?

sp.speaker: Patricia Wilcox
sp.p: No. You know so many people entered your life, you couldn't keep up with them. And, you know some lost parents and there were things like that. There were other girls who, there's another gal became a widow about the same time I did, and I had a tough time dealing with it, but then they wanted me to go take care of her. I didn't do it. I couldn't. I couldn't face her.

sp.speaker: Janice L. Friddle
sp.p: Yeah, that would have been difficult.

sp.speaker: Patricia Wilcox
sp.p: Yeah, they said, you know you might be able to help her and I thought, I can't help her. I can't even help myself, so.

sp.speaker: Jeremiah Mora
sp.p: How about your childhood friend that you enlisted with?

sp.speaker: Patricia Wilcox
sp.p: Well, she wound up in Mississippi doing radio work and she loved it, and then she wound up finally, she never went overseas, she went up to Chanute Field, Illinois where she was and I think she was at Peterson Field down here in Colorado Springs doing radio work. She got out quite a bit before I did. And what was so beautiful about her, her family was so heated. Her father had lost everything, everything he owned in the Depression. Everything. His store, his home, everything. And he didn't have any money to send her to school, but luckily she had the GI bill and she went to a fashion design school in Boston and she became vice president of a manufacturing company in Cincinnati that made children's clothes. She designed all their clothes. And she, she's married, she's a millionaire.

sp.speaker: Janice L. Friddle
sp.p: Wow. That's a great story.

sp.speaker: Patricia Wilcox
sp.p: Yeah. And she had - I remember one time when she told me during the Depression, the mother said to her there's nothing to eat now except some potato and I knew we need some fish. And they looked under all the rugs, under all the carpets looking for pennies, and they managed to scrape up 7 cents. And the mother said to her, the mother wouldn't go to the store and ask for 7 cents worth of fish, but Franny had to go. And ask for seven cents piece of fish.

sp.speaker: Janice L. Friddle
sp.p: Wow.

sp.speaker: Patricia Wilcox
sp.p: So, to her, this whole WAC thing was a great experience. I mean it changed her whole life.

sp.speaker: Janice L. Friddle
sp.p: I'd like take us back to Paris since that's where we left off with your war experience. And so you're working with a lot of newspaper people.

sp.speaker: Patricia Wilcox
sp.p: I'm working with a lot of newspaper men. and I'm having a great time. I'm going out all the time and exploring Paris and just having various adventures. You know I, oh I'll have to tell you about my trip to the Follies. One day a gal and I decided to go up to Compiegne, her brother was a major there and he was in charge of transportation so she could get a jeep whenever she wanted it, so we went to get on the jeep, decided to spend the weekend up at Compiegne, I don't know why. Just for old times sake. And we went up there. But on the way home we picked up a couple of fellahs that were bumming rides, and one of them was a, I think he was a, well he was a top sergeant. He came from Jackson, Mississippi. He was a married guy, and they suggested they take us for lunch at this hotel or something that he knew about. So we went to a hotel that was out in the country, and that's when I first had venison. And, anyway, I don't remember where he was stationed, but he would come into Paris once in awhile and he always would call me and take me out. He was a very, very nice guy. And he told me one time, he said, he was in the real estate business. He said, if you get our hands on as much as $500, let me handle it for you. He said, I'll buy you some real estate. Jackson, Mississippi is going to grow into a huge city. But I never got the $500. Janke: My mother was born in Jackson, Mississippi.

sp.speaker: Patricia Wilcox
sp.p: Was she really?

sp.speaker: Janice L. Friddle
sp.p: Yeah, she was.

sp.speaker: Patricia Wilcox
sp.p: Oh God. I went to the State Fair down there. You know, his name was Moses Stewart. He was a great guy. Well anyway, one night he was coming into town from wherever he was stationed, and he told me, he said you know if you're free, I want to take you to the Follies, Follies Burgees. Well, of course it's now gone because it was very shocking at that time. I mean the women came out topless and all this kind of thing. So we got to the Follies and I expected just sitting in a place just like an ordinary theater. But in the front row they had chairs, like armchairs with ashtrays beside them and you sat in the front row and all the comfort of the world, and that's where we wound up. He bought the best seats in the house. And we were there. And of course then all these ladies came trotting in, jiggling, and [LAUGHTER] and there was a master of ceremonies, and pretty soon after this parade of beautiful women had all passed by and off the stage, he leaned down and then there's a teeny little pair of pink panties. And he said, oh someone lost their panties. I think my friend was translating for me, because I didn't know - I knew French from high school, but I didn't know it that well. And, so he held up these little pink things that were like thongs really. And said, does anyone belong to these? And I got this sick feeling in my stomach, because suddenly he came over and he said, could these be yours? So, my friend said stand up. So all of sudden they had lights of the follies were on me, and I said no. No. Not mine. Then he said, well prove it. Well, we had underwear, all our underwear was khaki colored mind you. And the pants, what we call panties were more like bloomers except they didn't have elastic on the bottom, and the longer you had them, the longer they grew. I don't know what it was. The elastic got tighter around the waist, but the legs seemed to get longer. So anyway, I stood up in front of these, and here's all these millions of people, I mean balconies full of people and everything, and he said prove it. So I looked at Moses and he said pull up your skirts. And I pulled my skirts up and here are these khaki underwear [LAUGHTER] hanging down there, and everybody started laughing. Oh, I was so damned embarrassed, and I could have killed this guy. I really could have. I found a letter from him yesterday saying I hope you never forget your night in the follies. And, it made me laugh. I would have forgotten to tell you about that if it hadn't been that letter I read yesterday. But, anyway, and we had a great time. You know, I didn't meet many civilians. I just hung around mostly with the guys.

sp.speaker: Janice L. Friddle
sp.p: What did you - how much of the transformation of Paris and after the war did you get to see?

sp.speaker: Patricia Wilcox
sp.p: Well, on Tuesday nights there were no lights at all, so every Tuesday night was black out night. So, but before I left they were beginning - and of course I was there in the summertime too, and in August everybody in Paris they close their shops and they all go away you know. The whole country goes on vacation. Whether they go anywhere or they stay home, I don't know, but they're not in business. And, we, but there were plenty of nightclubs and the lido that I went to and all that kind of thing. And then this particular friend of mine that worked in the office, he was a darling boy. He was about five years younger then I but we stayed lifelong friends. And we would go down in the Latin Corridor where there was something, a little tiny Swiss Restaurant. And it would say bif steak. B-I-F S-T-E-A-K, I think was on the menu. So we'd have steak. And it was delicious. We found out later it was horse meat. [LAUGHTER] But we didn't know at that time. But we were pretty regular down there, and then one night he said to me, here's a place. Let's go in there and have a drink. So we went in. It turned out to be a house of prostitution. [LAUGHTER] We sat in the living room and all these girls were going upstairs and different people were hiding, and we had our drinks and then we left.

sp.speaker: Janice L. Friddle
sp.p: So during the course of your enlistment, you went from being I'm assuming somewhat of an innocent, New England family.

sp.speaker: Patricia Wilcox
sp.p: Yeah, I was. Yeah, very. Yes, I was. Janke: Young, raised a ...

sp.speaker: Patricia Wilcox
sp.p: Yeah, a good Catholic family, yeah. Janke: And you were exposed to some ...

sp.speaker: Patricia Wilcox
sp.p: To everything. Just about everything. I think I did go to church once. Emily was a Catholic and she insisted I go once to mass at the Cathedral of the Notre Dame which I'm glad I did because the music was just, it was fantastic. But I just had gotten away from that kind of thing totally. But, Paris itself, I mean you could just wander around and we'd meet characters. You know. I mean I remember one day meeting some old lady leaned out things said you Yankee and come in and talk to me. We went in and talked to her, and she told us stories about some of the characters on the street. That kind of thing. Went to the flea market. I mean we were just busy all the time. And then a lot of dating going on too, you know, but it was great. So, finally I met this gal and I had plenty of time, furlough time and one day I was saying that I had a couple of weeks furlough time. She said, so do I. And she said let's go to England. So we went - we signed up for a furlough and made arrangements to go to England. And going across the channel we met two other gals that were WACs and the four of us teamed up. And we went there and we stayed in a Red Cross place. I think it was in Barkley Square. And, we had a marvelous time. We were in a movie. We were extras in a movie. It was called "Between the Years" and the star was Michael Redgrave.

sp.speaker: Janice L. Friddle
sp.p: It's fun hearing your adventures. I'm curious as far as a writer in this time, can you think of a particular interview that you, or story that you wrote that was either just striking or it stayed with you?

sp.speaker: Patricia Wilcox
sp.p: No, not really. I wrote about so many men and their experiences that they've all jumbled together, you know, and I interviewed one when I was still in the States that had come from overseas that told me some strange stories. But, no I really can't think of anything. I wrote some articles for educational magazines, and I mean to me they were kind of boring. It was nothing that I really ever wrote that struck me.

sp.speaker: Janice L. Friddle
sp.p: What is the objective of the Army having you interview them?

sp.speaker: Patricia Wilcox
sp.p: Just, all these things were sent back to the States. I think I must have written articles that appeared in every newspaper from the smallest weekly to the biggest daily in the country. I mean, if he got promoted, if he won some distinction - it didn't matter what. You sent it back to the hometown or to the home city, and that way the folks at home knew what everybody was doing and where they were and what they were accomplishing, you know, and all that kind of thing. Janke: So you actually were the link between ...

sp.speaker: Patricia Wilcox
sp.p: Yeah. It was public relations, yeah. Yes.

sp.speaker: Janice L. Friddle
sp.p: Fascinating.

sp.speaker: Patricia Wilcox
sp.p: We did them by the hundreds.

sp.speaker: Janice L. Friddle
sp.p: I'm sure you impacted a great many lives that you have no ...

sp.speaker: Patricia Wilcox
sp.p: Probably. Yeah. Probably. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Janice L. Friddle
sp.p: So you're in Paris and you're having a good time working.

sp.speaker: Patricia Wilcox
sp.p: Yeah. And then I went on this furlough to - and we had a great time. We were in this movie with Michael Redgrave, and his wife was also an actress in it. I suppose by that time Vanessa, yeah there were a couple of other members of the family. I've forgotten who they are, but anyway they hadn't yet appeared on the stage as far as I know. And it was an all day thing, and we were just extras. You know, they would dance, Michael and his wife were dancing and we were sitting around having cocktails which turned out to be cold tea. And, we were all paid. I think we were paid seven or ten dollars for the day. I was going to keep it because he autographed it, but I wound up spending it. And then all of sudden while I was there, the Stars and Stripes came out. And we went to Scotland. Just England to Scotland. And all of a sudden the Stars and Stripes came out and I realized that I was eligible to go home. I had 32 points and they were sending 32 points down. You had points for your service, I mean overseas. When I was in France by the way, the French government gave us each $20 a month more than the government was paying us because of the high prices and things. The perfume was about all you could buy. And they also supplied us, everybody got something like four bottles of wine a month donated by the wineries. So if you had a boyfriend come to visit you at the hotel, and you wanted to, decided to stay in that day room, this beautiful living room place well you could open your bottle of wine. They had no, [UNINTELLIGIBLE] objection to that.

sp.speaker: Janice L. Friddle
sp.p: So you find out you're going to go home. Or you can?

sp.speaker: Patricia Wilcox
sp.p: Yes. So I went back to Paris and I packed my duds and I left there I think about December 10th. And I figured that I would be home by Christmas. And that was a lot, because that was an entirely different story. We got there - we went to place in Mohave called - all these camps where they were deploying people were named after cigarettes. I mean there was Camp Chesterfield. I was at Camp Philip Morris. And it was December, it was snowing, it was mud and they were tar paper barracks, a horrible place. And you had the coal stoves to fight with you know that were in the middle of barrack. And I had never before realized that there were black women in the Women's Army Corps. Never had seen one. Never had heard of one. Never. And guess what street they were off! They used the Army alphabet to name the streets, what they use over the radio, Abel, Baker, Charlie, Dog, you know. They were on Dog street. All the black girls were on dog street. That really infuriated me, but having been in the deep South I knew exactly how they treated those people which stunned me as a Yankee. But I never saw any of them. They never ate with us. They were totally, you know ...

sp.speaker: Janice L. Friddle
sp.p: Segregated.

sp.speaker: Patricia Wilcox
sp.p: Totally segregated. So we were there and the first thing that happened was the orderly room caught fire and we almost lost all our records and we thought my God, we're going to be here the rest of our lives. And then finally, the ship arrived. And we went down to look at this ship, well all the fellahs had been gambling for all this time, and they all had so much money. And they would pay you, I don't know how much money I made. You were allowed to bring something like $500 back. I mean the government had sense enough to know the people were gambling. And so, one of these fellahs had thousands of dollars. So anyway, one would say how much do you have? I didn't have anything. I had spent all my money. I never saved a dime. So I said, well I don't have anything. Well I'll give you $200 if you'll you know take my $300, or something like that. So we all made a few bucks. So we got onto the ship and it was an old French ship, at one time it started life before World War I as a cruiser, a cruise ship. And it was called the Athos, A- T -H-O-S. It was after one of the three musketeers. And we got on. It had an all civilian French crew out of Marseilles. And at first it was great. We had tablecloths. We had bowls of shrimp. I mean a luxury ship. It just seemed perfect. I was in a room with just four others. I think there were three other girls, we had the top [UNINTELLIGIBLE]. And everything was just great until we had been out to sea about four days. And all of sudden we were hit by this hideous, horrible hurricane. It was a sight of cyclone proportions. We lost all of the life boats. The waves were coming up over the top. The windows were giving in. The food was almost entirely washed away. The radio shack caught fire. There was somebody imprisoned in another room where the walls collapsed. And I was upstairs in the library. They called it the library, it was kind of a social room. And the piano had started - it was an upright and it started rolling back and forth, you know and I though I'm going back to my room because this is getting pretty, you know the piano was rather large and you didn't want to be hit by the piano. And I went back and I was lying there, trying to read and all of a sudden I looked and I love peppermint patties. And I looked, this peppermint patty went flying by me with one of my earrings stuck in it. [LAUGHTER]

sp.speaker: Patricia Wilcox
sp.p: Well the next thing I knew, everybody was back in the cabins and they made us all go out to the halls to lie down. We couldn't sleep in the cabins any longer, it was too dangerous. And finally the ship was rocking. It was a terrible, terrible ordeal. It almost, it went over 45 degree rolls. And so in order to save the ship, all the personnel had to go into the hold. And that was quite an experience because all they had were these greasy ladders that went down and down and down into the bottom. And the civilian sailors were helping grab you so that you wouldn't slip on these ladders. And we all went down into that place. We had to walk through, go through the kitchen. The stove had tom loose, that was flying back and force. The water, I don't know what happened to it. I was almost knee deep in water. And there were orange peels, garbage allover the place that you had to wade through, and I know in back of me was this girl and she was like we're going to die, we're all going to die. I said, oh shut up. You know. Anyway, and then they put us into these different like little alleys or something. I don't know they - and you'd sit down and one minute you'd look at your feet would be way up in the air, and the next minute you'd be down here. I mean that's how badly it was rocking. So that kept up for oh, 24 - 30 hours.

sp.speaker: Janice L. Friddle
sp.p: Wow.

sp.speaker: Patricia Wilcox
sp.p: So after that we had one meal a day, and it was either Brussel sprouts and a piece of cheese. So we spent Christmas there, Christmas Eve. And the wind had blown us. We were off the coast of New Finland when this all hit. And this wind blew this totally disabled ship. The boiler had almost burst. Everything was - the engines were gone. Everything. It blew this helpless thing with all these 2,000 GIs and 212 WACs, it blew us all the way from the coast of New Finland to the Azo Islands off Portugal.

sp.speaker: Janice L. Friddle
sp.p: My gosh.

sp.speaker: Patricia Wilcox
sp.p: And there we were. And we weren't allowed - we thought we'd be able to go ashore one of the islands, but no they wouldn't let us go to shore on the islands. They certainly weren't going to let the men go ashore on the islands. But the men use to jump over the deck and swim ashore. But then the islanders would come out with pineapples and different things like that so we were able to get fresh fruit and of course they also came out with bottles of, I think it was 200 proof rum that the guys would get, and oh New Years Eve on that ship was terrible. Those guys were absolutely, oh they were drunk. They were fighting the officers and, it was a real jamboree. And no one was killed, but a lot of people had their teeth all knocked out or arms broken or legs broken and that kind of thing. And I had, it was the master sergeant in my room and when I went back and I saw the peppermint patty flying, this girl came back and she was just quivering and crying and I said, what's the matter? She said we're in a shipwreck. And I said well I'm sure we're going to be alright. I had great faith in the ocean. I figured oh hell, I can swim. It never dawned on me that this thing would be 20 below zero and I'd be frozen to death in ten seconds. That never occurred to me, but I was going to be able to swim near land for help. But she had been on a ship that was very famous at the time, it was the called the Marrow Castle, Marrow Castle was in Havana. And at that time people from New York used to go over to Havana to gamble for a weekend cruise. And she was on this Marrow Castle ship when on the way home it caught fire and the captain died and the whole thing just beached in New Jersey someplace. And they lost hundreds of passengers in this thing. And it was up on the beach and I know all kinds of people, including my parents went down to look at it, you know to see this sight. And she had been on that and escaped from it, so she exactly knew and she was expecting the same thing. And she got so bad they finally had to put her in a padded cell.

sp.speaker: Janice L. Friddle
sp.p: Really?

sp.speaker: Patricia Wilcox
sp.p: Yeah. There were two girls that just went out of their minds.

sp.speaker: Janice L. Friddle
sp.p: Wow.

sp.speaker: Patricia Wilcox
sp.p: Last I heard she was still ... We were onboard, we were at sea 31 days.

sp.speaker: Janice L. Friddle
sp.p: Out of the 31 you were in this sort of holding flotation for a storm for how long?

sp.speaker: Patricia Wilcox
sp.p: Yeah. Well, after we got to the Athos, I'd forgotten how long we were in Athos, but then one of the gals, it was a ship very famous aircraft carrier called the Enterprise, I think they called it the Big-E. And the daughter of the vice commander of that ship was one of the WACs. And somebody, one of the offICers that went ashore called up Walden Winchell who was able to announce - it was [UNINTELLIGIBLE]. It was in the papers, 212 WACs drown at sea, you know and all that kind of thing. They had a lot of publicity about it. But he called up Walden Winchell to announce to tell them that we were okay, that we were in the Athos. And then the government sent out telegrams to all our families. It just says in Athos safe, don't try to contact.

sp.speaker: Janice L. Friddle
sp.p: Wow.

sp.speaker: Patricia Wilcox
sp.p: So then the Enterprise came and it took our bunch aboard and that's when I looked out window and there was another ship that had been disabled. It was a ship for blacks, there were 400 soldiers on that one. That had been disabled too. And I looked out and there's the Big E and there are these black men climbing cargo nets. [LAUGHTER]

sp.speaker: Patricia Wilcox
sp.p: And I thought, oh my God. I don't want to leave the Athos, I want to stay here. I was terrified that I'd have to climb those cargo nets because I would be so frightened. But anyway, we didn't have to do that. I mean they put down steps, jumped into a boat and we went to the Enterprise. We were treated like royalty. We had turkey dinner the first night and then we got off, that was the end of it.

sp.speaker: Janice L. Friddle
sp.p: Of all of your involvement in the War, what is the thing that sticks with you the most?

sp.speaker: Patricia Wilcox
sp.p: The most? Well, one is the, well, that shipwreck sticks with me most as far as the experiences. And of course my short lived marriage stays with me a lot and because I'm still in touch with his family you know. And, I don't know, just different things. People that I met pop into my mind, and as I told you I have a lifelong friendship with this young man that had been my officer and when this development first started being built he was working, he was doing advertising work and he said to me, I think we were living in Denver at that time, he said you need a bigger house. He said I'm going to make it happen. He said, I'm going to give you my GI bill because I had used mine to buy our first house. My husband had given his to his folks, and so when he gave me is, of course I gave it back to him later as soon as the house got built. When he really needed it. When he called one day and said, what about my GI bill? This is years and years later. And I said oh that's been paid off a long time, so. So that's about it. [END OF INTERVIEW]
